pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, 
Inc. 
) 
) 
) 
 
Docket No. ER26-3552-000 
 
COMMENTS OF THE SOLAR ENERGY INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION 
 
Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA)2 submits these 
comments supporting the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s (MISO) filing 
proposing revisions to establish the Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement 
(ZGIA).3 In addition to establishing the ZGIA, MISO’s ZGIA Proposal would establish a study 
process and operational requirements, and market and resource adequacy rules to accommodate 
Zero-Injection Generation Resources (ZG Resources) that intend to serve load interconnecting at 
the same substation as the Generating Facility. MISO’s proposal represents a just and reasonable 
step toward addressing the resource adequacy issues posed by the rapid addition of large loads. 
SEIA supports MISO’s ZGIA Proposal and urges the Commission to accept it.4 
 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.213 (2026). 
2 The comments contained in this filing represent the position of SEIA as a trade organization on behalf of the solar 
industry, but do not necessarily reflect the views of any particular member with respect to any issue. 
3 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement, Docket 
No. ER26-3552-000 (Aug. 18, 2026) (ZGIA Proposal). 
4 Capitalized terms not defined in these comments have the same meaning as in the Tariff or the ZGIA Proposal, as 
applicable.

2 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
The MISO region faces unprecedented growth in energy demand, driven largely by data 
centers, next-generation manufacturing, and electrification.5 The Commission recognized these 
challenges in its Show Cause Order in Docket No. EL26-70-000, which raised concerns about, 
among other things, the absence of generator interconnection service and study processes 
tailored to generation serving co-located or electrically proximate large load.6 The ZGIA 
Proposal is the first in a series of filings MISO intends to make to address those concerns.7 If 
approved, it would address generation serving co-located load at the same substation—the co-
location subset of the Show Cause Order’s concerns—by establishing an expedited 
interconnection pathway while preserving MISO’s interconnection queue and planning 
processes.8 As MISO has indicated, other issues, including transmission service for co-located 
and proximate loads and the integration of electrically proximate generation, would be addressed 
in subsequent filings.9 SEIA supports the ZGIA Proposal as a just and reasonable first step 
toward addressing these co-location and large load interconnection challenges. 
 
 
5 See MISO, 2026 Reliability Imperative Report, at 2 (Feb. 2026), available at: 
https://cdn.misoenergy.org/2026%20Reliability%20Imperative%20Report744320.pdf. 
6 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal 
Power Act, 195 FERC ¶ 61,212. PP 94, 97, 113 (2026) (Show Cause Order). 
7 See ZGIA Proposal, Transmittal Letter at 5–6 (explaining that “[t]he present filing represents the first of this 
series” of filings MISO intends to submit to address the concerns raised in the Show Cause Order). 
8 See id. at 1–2 (explaining that MISO “submits proposed revisions to its [Tariff] to establish a Zero Injection 
Generator Interconnection Agreement (‘ZGIA’), associated study process and operational requirements, and market 
and resource adequacy rules to accommodate [ZG Resources]”). 
9 See id. at 7, 10–11 (explaining that MISO “chose not to incorporate a ‘proximate’ load solution in this initial 
filing” and that MISO “will continue to develop the LARS process through the LLWG” and “expects to submit the 
LARS filing by November 16, 2026, or earlier”).

3 
II. 
COMMENTS 
A. 
The ZGIA Proposal Appropriately Limits Zero Injection Generation 
Interconnection Service to Co-Located Configurations, Addressing 
Deliverability Concerns. 
 
Under MISO’s existing interconnection framework, a resource that injects power onto the 
Transmission System must demonstrate deliverability through the Definitive Planning Phase 
(DPP). Deliverability is a prerequisite to receiving full capacity accreditation and marketable 
Zonal Resource Credits.10 However, under the ZGIA proposal, a project developed under a 
ZGIA would not grant deliverability rights. The ZGIA Proposal limits Zero Injection Generation 
Interconnection Service (ZG Interconnection Service) to co-located configurations in which ZG 
Resources and the Zero Injection Generation Associated Load (ZG Associated Load) would be 
located at the same substation and voltage level, with no injection beyond the interconnecting 
substation. Because the ZG Resource would not inject onto the broader Transmission System, 
the co-location design would avoid the need for a deliverability analysis.11 Under the ZGIA 
Proposal, ZG Interconnection Service would not grant injection rights or deliverability, and 
MISO would require that no Network Upgrades be needed beyond the interconnecting substation 
(except limited System Protection Facilities).12 A ZG Resource that would trigger broader 
Network Upgrades would not qualify and would instead need to proceed through the DPP.13 The 
 
10 See MISO Tariff, Module E-1, Section 69A (establishing accreditation and capacity credit framework for 
Planning Resources); see also Show Cause Order at PP 94, 113 (discussing the need for generator interconnection 
service tailored to generation serving co-located load and recognizing that limited or no injection may reduce the 
need for Network Upgrades).   
11 See ZGIA Proposal, Transmittal Letter at 26 (explaining that “[i]t is not necessary to include this limited product 
in DPP studies because its lack of injection prevents it from having impacts on the broader Transmission System”). 
12 See ZGIA Proposal, Proposed Tariff, Attachment X, Section 3.2.5.1 (establishing ZG Interconnection Service 
requirements including same-substation and same-voltage-level limitations); see also id., Transmittal Letter at 25–
27 (explaining that limiting injection onto the broader Transmission System is the foundational feature of ZG 
Interconnection Service and that the requirement that no Network Upgrades be needed beyond the interconnecting 
substation acts as a key guardrail). 
13 See ZGIA Proposal, Transmittal Letter at 26 (explaining that if Network Upgrades were needed beyond the 
interconnecting substation, “that would both call into question the lack of injection and raise cost-shifting risk for 
other Interconnection Customers”); see also id. at 31 (“Interconnection Requests with such impacts are better

4 
co-location requirement, coupled with the strict load-following obligation, would confine the 
ZGIA to arrangements with minimal Transmission System impact—generation would be 
physically co-located with the load it would serve and would reduce output in real time if that 
load decreased,14 ensuring that the ZG Resource does not inject onto the Transmission System.15 
These guardrails prevent ZG Resources from bypassing the deliverability requirements that 
apply to all other interconnecting generation, avoiding potential cost-shifting to other 
Interconnection Customers and preserving the integrity of the DPP queue.16 
The ZGIA Proposal’s resource adequacy provisions would further address related 
concerns by limiting ZG Resource accreditation to the lesser of each resource’s applicable 
accreditation or the ZG Associated Load’s requirement and by requiring associated Zonal 
Resource Credits (ZRCs) to be used with the ZG Associated Load in the applicable Load Serving 
Entity’s Fixed Resource Adequacy Plan or Reliability Based Demand Curve Opt-Out.17 For 
SEIA, these limitations are important because they would maintain a level playing field by 
ensuring ZG Resources receive capacity credit only for the load they actually serve, rather than 
competing with fully deliverable Planning Resources for transferable capacity value. 
 
processed through the DPP where they can study in a cluster with other Interconnection Requests with potential 
impacts on the broader Transmission System”). 
14 See ZGIA Proposal, Transmittal Letter at 26 (explaining that “if there is a decrease in the ZG Associated Load’s 
demand, it is important to correspondingly reduce the output of the ZG Resource to prevent power from flowing out 
onto the Transmission System”). 
15 See id. at 12–15, 18–20, 25–29 (describing the same-substation and same-voltage limitations, injection 
restrictions, resource adequacy guardrails, and DPP treatment, and explaining that the “limited distance over which 
energy would need to be—and is permitted to—flow allows for a more targeted study”). 
16 See SEIA’s Comments in Response to MISO’s Updated ZGIA Proposal (Mar. 23, 2026), available at: 
https://www.misoenergy.org/engage/stakeholder-feedback/2026/pac-zgia-proposal-framework-pac-2024-4-
20260225/. 
17 See SEIA’s Comments in Response to MISO’s Updated ZGIA Proposal (Mar. 23, 2026) (urging MISO to “create 
guardrails by making clear that any ZRCs associated with a ZGIA resource are non-transferable”), available at: 
https://www.misoenergy.org/engage/stakeholder-feedback/2026/pac-zgia-proposal-framework-pac-2024-4-
20260225/; see also Clean Grid Alliance Comments Submitted by David Sapper (May 5, 2026) (raising concerns 
regarding accreditation impacts of adding ZGIA resources to direct loss of load modeling), available at: 
https://www.misoenergy.org/engage/stakeholder-feedback/2026/llwg-zgia-proposal-framework-pac-2024-4b-
20260420/.

5 
 
B. 
The ZGIA Proposal Supports Speed to Reliable Power While Preserving 
System Integrity. 
 
Under the ZGIA Proposal, ZG Interconnection Service would be available only where the 
Generating Facility and the ZG Associated Load are at the same substation and voltage level.18 
MISO considered and rejected broader scopes, including electrically proximate configurations, 
based on stakeholder concerns about injection control, unconstrained power flows, and potential 
state retail service conflicts.19 By drawing the boundary at the substation level, MISO would 
limit ZG Interconnection Service to configurations where injection controls can be effectively 
verified,20 and the expedited 90-day study process would be well-suited to these limited 
configurations.21 
A critical feature of this process is that MISO has designed the ZGIA study track to 
operate independently of the DPP.22 As MISO indicates, ZGIA studies would use a separate 
model base that does not include pending DPP interconnection requests,23 and ZGIA approvals 
would not be added to ongoing DPP studies. MISO would reconcile both sets of results in the 
next MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (MTEP) base case.24 This structural separation 
 
18 ZGIA Proposal, Proposed Tariff, Attachment X, Section 3.2.5.1. 
19 ZGIA Proposal, Transmittal Letter at 7. 
20 See id. at 28 (explaining that “an examination of the electrical connection between the Generating Facility, ZG 
Associated Load, and the Transmission system, and the proposed control equipment becomes a critical aspect of the 
study”). 
21 See id. at 14 (“[A] separate, expedited study process and corresponding form of Interconnection Service is both 
feasible and responsive to the Commission’s directive to address the needs of certain loads, including large loads 
associated with data centers.”). 
22 See id. at 15 (“[T]his insulates existing DPP projects from negative impacts or cost shifts due to the existence of 
the ZGIA process.”). 
23 See id. (explaining that “[b]efore every ZGIA cycle, all Interconnection Requests with a GIA approved since the 
last base case was created will be added to the base case for the ZGIA cycle but will not be added in any ongoing 
DPP studies” and that ZGIA studies will not use available transmission capacity in DPP studies or adversely affect 
DPP projects). 
24 See id. (explaining that ZGIA studies will not use available transmission capacity in DPP studies or adversely 
affect DPP projects).

6 
supports ZG Resources proceeding on a 90-day study timeline without consuming transmission 
capacity reserved for DPP projects or increasing costs for projects already in the queue.25 
 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
MISO’s ZGIA proposal represents a just and reasonable step toward addressing the 
resource adequacy issues posed by the rapid addition of large loads. SEIA respectfully urges the 
Commission to accept MISO’s ZGIA Proposal.  
Respectfully submitted, 
 
 
 
/s/ Melissa Alfano 
 
Melissa Alfano  
Senior Director of Energy Markets and Counsel  
Solar Energy Industries Association  
1425 K St NW Ste. 1000  
Washington, DC 20005  
(202) 566-2873  
malfano@seia.org   
 
 
Dated: September 8, 2026 
 
 
25 See id. (“[T]he standing MISO DPP three phase and ERAS processes will not be impacted by ZGIA, as ZGIA will 
not be utilizing any available transmission capacity in those studies.”).

CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE 
 
I hereby certify that I have this day served the foregoing document upon each person 
designated on the official service list compiled by the Secretary in this proceeding. 
Dated at Washington, DC, this 8th day of September, 2026. 
 
 
 
/s/ Melissa Alfano 
 
Melissa Alfano
